implementation_notes: C++ has the richest exception semantics of the languages here and therefore the most ways to abuse them. The characteristic forms are a custom exception type used as a loop break and caught two frames up; a `std::optional`/`std::expected` ignored in favour of a throw; and RAII interaction — throwing out of a constructor leaves already-constructed members destructed, which is correct but means an exception used as an early exit can silently run a whole destructor chain. C++23's `std::expected` is the standard-blessed replacement for the result case and removes the main justification for the throw-as-result pattern. C++ Core Guidelines' advice is the local rule to cite: use exceptions for error reporting and propagate them up a call tree only when the function cannot handle them.
idiom_name: throw for control flow; exceptions across noexcept boundaries
pitfalls: Throwing out of a constructor runs every constructed member's destructor, so an exception used as an early exit can have side effects nobody modelled.
Swallowing an exception in a destructor with `catch (...)` hides the original exception and is exactly the quenchability problem.
`noexcept` functions that throw terminate the program, which makes an accidental control-flow throw catastrophic rather than merely slow.
Using `throw;` to rethrow inside a `catch` that also does cleanup hides which exception is being propagated.
